text: Empathy is a masculine capacity. What women have is sympathy. These are completely different things. Let me explain. Empathy is trying to examine the way that someone feels about their situation. And sympathy is the way that a person's situation makes you feel. Does that make sense? Remember the guy who used the fabricated study to claim that 97% of women would rather spend 48 hours in jail than admit they were wrong? Well, I came across another gem from his channel. This time he claims that women do not have empathy, that empathy is a masculine capacity, and what women have instead is sympathy. So let's begin with the definitions. There is no single definition of empathy used by every psychologist, but it is generally understood as the ability to understand or share another person's feelings. It is commonly divided into two parts. Cognitive sympathy is understanding what another person thinks or feels from their perspective. Emotional empathy is sharing or reflecting what that person is feeling. Sympathy is slightly different. It means feeling concern or sorrow for another person without necessarily sharing their emotions. So his definition of empathy is not completely wrong. It is reasonably close to cognitive empathy, but he ignores emotional empathy. And his definition of sympathy is not accurate. Sympathy is not simply how another person's situation makes you feel, and it is not inherently about yourself. Psychologists actually use a different term for self-focused reaction to someone else's suffering, personal distress. But definitions aside, what happens when researchers actually compare men and women? The results depend on how empathy is measured. When people answer questionnaires about their own empathy, women generally score somewhat higher than men. But the difference is modest, and the scores overlap substantially, meaning men and women are generally much more similar than different. However, questionnaires measure what people say about themselves. Men and women may describe themselves differently, for example, because society generally expects women to be more caring and men to be less emotional. So what about tests where people actually have to understand someone else? One study tested more than 312,000 people across 57 countries. Participants looked at photographs of people's eyes and tried to identify what those people were thinking or feeling. Women scored slightly higher on average. This female advantage was statistically significant in 36 of the 57 countries, while no country showed a statistically significant male advantage. Of course, looking at photographs of someone's eyes cannot measure every aspect of real-life empathy, but it is one of the largest studies of people's ability to understand another person's mental state, precisely the ability he claims women lack. Another study showed 521 participants' videos of people describing emotional experiences. After each video, participants rated how they felt and how much compassion they felt for the speaker. Women reported stronger emotional reactions and more compassion. But when participants answered questions about what the speakers were thinking, men and women were equally accurate. So is it true that women have no empathy and that empathy is only a masculine capacity? Absolutely not. On questionnaires, women generally report more empathy than men. On tests of people's ability to understand others, researchers usually find either little difference or small female advantage. And regarding sympathy, women also tend to score higher in concern and sympathy for others. The evidence is not that men have empathy while women have sympathy. Women demonstrate both and on average, frequently score somewhat higher in both. That doesn't make every woman more empathetic than every man. The differences are averages. They are generally quite small and there's substantial overlap between the sexes. But the idea that women are literally incapable of empathy is just absurd.
